analysis.one_liner: Taxes imported crude oil, refined products, and petrochemicals whenever world oil prices fall below a floor.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee the day it was introduced, never received a hearing or vote, and died when the 103rd Congress ended on January 3, 1995.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would put a fee on foreign oil. Whenever the world price of oil was below $25 a barrel, importers would pay the difference on every barrel of imported crude they sold, plus similar fees on imported refined products and petrochemical feedstocks. The fee would shrink to zero when world prices rose above the floor, and the thresholds would rise with inflation. Domestic oil would be exempt.
analysis.who_benefits: Domestic oil producers gain a guaranteed price floor: imported oil could never undercut $25 a barrel (or $27.50 for refined products), letting U.S. producers charge more. The Treasury also collects the fee. Buyers in the petrochemical and refining businesses could deduct the tax from their taxable income.

how_it_helps.text: Imposes an excise tax on the first sale or use in the United States of imported crude oil, refined petroleum products, and petrochemical feedstocks or derivatives.

Sets the crude oil tax at the excess of $25 per barrel over the average internationally traded oil price, and $27.50 per barrel for refined products, so the tax grows as world prices fall and disappears when they rise above the floor.
Excludes crude oil produced from wells in the United States, so only foreign oil is taxed.
Adjusts the $25 and $27.50 thresholds for inflation each year after 1993.
Makes the imported-oil tax deductible for income tax purposes, so business buyers can subtract it from taxable income.

analysis.who_pays: Households and businesses that buy gasoline, heating oil, and products made from petrochemicals. Whenever world oil sold below $25 a barrel, the fee would push the U.S. price of imported oil up to that floor, and those costs would flow into pump prices, heating bills, and the price of plastics and chemicals. Oil importers and refiners dependent on foreign crude would pay the fee directly.

drawbacks.text: The tax fills the gap between world prices and $25 a barrel, so it would directly raise the U.S. price of imported oil — and with it gasoline, heating fuel, and goods made from petrochemicals — in any period when world oil sold below that floor.
Imported petrochemical feedstocks and derivatives would be taxed on a barrel-equivalent basis, raising input costs for U.S. plastics and chemical manufacturers.

The bill protects domestic producers from cheaper foreign oil rather than encouraging them to compete on cost; the fee is designed to disappear exactly when foreign oil is cheap enough to help consumers.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill would raise revenue and could reduce dependence on foreign oil, which supporters framed as energy security. But the mechanism is a price floor: it transfers money from anyone who buys fuel to domestic oil producers precisely when world markets offer cheaper oil. Consumers would pay the bill, and the deductibility provision lets business buyers soften their own share. The costs fall broadly on ordinary people; the benefits fall narrowly on domestic producers.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in the House Ways and Means Committee from the day it was introduced until the Congress ended, never getting a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote.

narrative.text: Rep. William Jefferson of Louisiana introduced the bill on February 4, 1993, and it was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means the same day.
The committee never took it up; the bill's entire recorded history is introduction, sponsor introductory remarks, and referral to committee.
It died without ever reaching the House floor when the 103rd Congress ended on January 3, 1995.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Consumers and businesses that buy fuel: the fee that would have raised their gasoline, heating, and petrochemical costs whenever world oil fell below $25 a barrel never became law. Oil importers also kept access to cheaper foreign crude.

for.name: Rep. William Jefferson
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Energy Security Tax Act and delivered introductory remarks on the House floor.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on February 4, 1993 and took no further action — no hearing, markup, or vote was ever scheduled.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and all five cosponsors were Democrats, but no vote was ever taken, so the partisan shape of opposition is not recorded.

industries.note: The fee guarantees imported oil cannot sell below $25 a barrel ($27.50 for refined products), so domestic producers could charge more whenever world prices fell below the floor. The money comes out of household fuel bills.

industries.industry: Oil importers and refiners using imported crude
industries.note: They would pay the fee on every imported barrel, raising their costs. Their interest in keeping cheap foreign oil flowing runs alongside consumers' interest in lower fuel prices.

Imported petrochemical feedstocks and derivatives would be taxed on a barrel-equivalent basis, raising input costs for plastics and chemical manufacturing. Cheaper feedstocks benefit these firms and, downstream, consumers of their products.
